summary: At Isaac's weaning feast Sarah demands that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away, and Abraham does so with grief; an angel leads Hagar to water and Ishmael survives. The scene then shifts to heaven, where Mastêmâ proposes a severe test of Abraham's attachment to Isaac.
whyItMatters: The chapter holds the cost of defining Isaac's inheritance beside God's care for Ishmael, and it prepares the reader for the trial narrated next.

context.author: Within the book, the angel of the presence dictates the account to Moses; the historical writer is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through Moses in the book’s frame; the specific first historical audience is not identified.
context.date: The narrative places the revelation at Sinai; the historical Hebrew work is usually dated to the second century BCE, without an established exact year.
context.setting: Abraham's household, the wilderness near Beersheba and Paran, and a heavenly conversation about Abraham.
context.literaryForm: Family crisis and wilderness rescue followed by a heavenly test prologue.

before.text: Isaac has been born and Abraham’s household has celebrated his promised arrival.

here.text: A feast turns into Hagar and Ishmael’s displacement and rescue, then a heavenly proposal to test Abraham.

after.text: The proposed test becomes an order to offer Isaac, but an angel stops the killing and a ram is offered instead.

outline.heading: Isaac’s feast and Sarah’s demand
outline.note: The celebration exposes conflict over inheritance.

outline.heading: Hagar and Ishmael sent into the wilderness
outline.note: God promises a future for Ishmael, but the water runs out.

outline.heading: An angel shows water and Ishmael grows
outline.note: The child survives and begins a family of his own.

outline.heading: Mastêmâ proposes a test
outline.note: Heavenly voices assess Abraham’s past trials and his love for Isaac.

keyVerses.text: And an angel of God, one of the holy ones, said unto her, 'Why weepest thou, Hagar? Arise take the child, and hold him in thine hand; for God hath heard thy voice, and hath seen the child.'
keyVerses.why: The angel addresses Hagar directly and says both her voice and the child have been seen and heard.

keyVerses.text: And the prince Mastêmâ came and said before God, 'Behold, Abraham loves Isaac his son, and he delights in him above all things else; bid him offer him as a burnt-offering on the altar, and Thou wilt see if he will do this command, and Thou wilt know if he is faithful in everything wherein Thou dost try him.
keyVerses.why: Mastêmâ's proposal sets up the next chapter's disturbing test without yet narrating it.

questions.question: Why does Sarah demand that Hagar and Ishmael leave?
questions.answer: She sees Ishmael during Isaac’s feast and says Hagar’s son must not share Isaac’s inheritance. The account names jealousy and inheritance but does not make the expulsion painless for Abraham or Hagar.

questions.question: Does God’s instruction to Abraham mean Hagar’s suffering is unimportant?
questions.answer: The narrative reports the instruction and also lingers over Hagar’s thirst, fear, and tears in the wilderness. An angel addresses her and reveals water; those details should be kept in view rather than treating her as merely a plot device.

questions.question: What does “bondwoman” mean in Sarah’s demand?
questions.answer: It is this edition’s term for an enslaved woman in Abraham’s household, here Hagar. Sarah uses that status to argue about her son’s inheritance; the text’s social hierarchy should be named rather than softened away.

questions.question: What future is promised for Ishmael?
questions.answer: God says he will become a great nation because he is Abraham’s son. After Hagar finds water, the boy grows, becomes an archer, and has a family; the chapter does not end with his death in the wilderness.

questions.question: How does the angel respond to Hagar?
questions.answer: The angel tells her to rise and hold the child because God has heard her and seen him. She then sees a well, fills the bottle, and gives Ishmael water.

questions.question: Who proposes the later offering of Isaac?
questions.answer: The chapter says Mastêmâ asks God to command Abraham to offer Isaac as a burnt offering to test him. The proposal is reported in a heavenly scene; it is not a command for human readers to imitate.

questions.question: Why list Abraham’s earlier trials before the next episode?
questions.answer: The speech recalls migration, famine, wealth, Sarai’s seizure, circumcision, and the sending away of Hagar and Ishmael. It frames the coming event as another test of a person already called faithful.

glossary.def: An enslaved woman; the term applied to Hagar in the inheritance dispute.
No longer nursing; Isaac’s weaning is marked by a household feast.
